approachQuestion.prompt: An access code consists of digits. Each token is the decimal representation of an integer from 1 through 26, with no leading zero. Count ways to split the entire code into valid tokens, modulo 1000000007. Examples: "121" → 3 ([1,2,1], [12,1], [1,21]); "101" → 1; "06" → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ n=code.length ≤ 200000; characters are decimal digits. Return only the modular count.

options.text: Start with one way for the empty prefix and one or zero for the first digit according to whether it is nonzero. For each later digit, add the previous-prefix count if this single digit is valid and the two-prefixes-back count if the last two digits form 10 through 26. Keep just those two counts.
options.feedback: A valid split ends in exactly one or two digits. The categories are disjoint, and zero can appear only inside 10 or 20.

options.text: Apply the same one-digit and two-digit recurrence but store the count for every prefix.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: Treat every single digit including zero as a valid token, while still accepting pairs 10 through 26.
options.feedback: For "10", this counts [1,0] in addition to [10], but zero is not a token.

options.text: Always take a valid two-digit token whenever possible; otherwise take a single digit, counting only that split.
options.feedback: For "121", it counts only [12,1], missing [1,2,1] and [1,21].

feedback.reason: Derive counting transitions from disjoint legal token endings and reject isolated zero digits.
details: Scan code once with two saved prefix counts and a temporary next count. Inspect digits by index and numeric character comparison, without substrings, retaining counts modulo 1000000007.

For code 121, prefix counts are 1,1,2,3 including the empty prefix. Legal one- and two-digit endings are disjoint. Zero cannot stand alone: 101 has one split and 06 none. Full prefix history is unnecessary without reconstruction.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Scan code once with two saved prefix counts and a temporary next count. Inspect digits by index and numeric character comparison, without substrings, retaining counts modulo 1000000007. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=n. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: A fixed number of validity checks and modular additions per digit use two prior counts.
details: Each digit requires a fixed number of validity checks and modular additions. Only two prior counts and temporaries are retained; no split strings or recursive calls are created.
“O(N²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Only the one-digit and two-digit endings are checked at each position, not all earlier split points.
“O(N) time, O(N) auxiliary space”: The fixed method retains two preceding counts, not all prefix counts.
“O(log(N+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The algorithm scans all digits; there is no binary search or repeated halving.
